body.text: In the popular imagination George Sand and Frederick Chopin form a legendary pair, key exemplars of the High Romanticism of their age. Check your Wikipedia and you’ll see how often they’ve been linked together in diaries, memoirs, biographies, fictions and, in our time, films, television and YouTube. But while Chopin’s music forms a significant part of the classical repertoire, Sand is too often portrayed simply as his muse or helpmeet.

It was a Eugene Delacroix painting that ushered in the depictions that differ so greatly from the actual nature of their relationship. In Delacroix’s portrayal, Chopin is at his piano on the right while Sand, in feminine attire, is seated at bottom left embroidering what looks like a velvet cloth.

This concocted, romanticised domestic harmony is what Fiona Sampson sets out to demolish in her new biography, Becoming George. “To become George Sand required will, imagination and chutzpah,” she writes. “In an era when both revolutionary and traditional forces were pulling at the social fabric within which she lived, she managed to emerge as one of the boldest precursors of that perhaps final hope modernity holds out: that we might choose what we become.”

The woman who eventually styled herself as George Sand was born Amantine-Aurore-Lucile Dupin de Francueil on 1 July 1804, her name shortened at some stage to Aurore Dupin. The time of her birth is notable in two ways. First, France had transformed from a republic when she was conceived to an empire when she was born. As Sampson defines it, this was a period of tension between the ruptures of the French Revolution and a reassertion of traditional values under Napoleon’s dictatorship — a tension that was mirrored in her parentage.

Her father was a dashing, aristocratic army officer serving under Napoleon when he married Sophie-Victoire, his older, working-class Parisienne paramour a month before the baby was due. By all accounts it was a loving relationship and Maurice Dupin de Francuel a doting father to the child until his early death in an accident. Aurore grew up on Nohant, the rural family estate, under the effective custody of her grandmother, and there were tensions enough there, complicated further by a son Maurice had fathered by another woman before he took up with Sophie-Victoire, who had herself given birth to a girl before meeting Maurice.

When Aurore reached her teens her grandmother sent her to a convent to be properly educated. At first desperately homesick for Nohant, she soon adjusted to convent life, making friends there and blossoming intellectually while committed to the religiosity the nuns succeeded in inculcating in their charges. Home again at Nohant, and following months of nursing her dying grandmother, she remained an innocent, ripe for romance and, thus, an early marriage. The eventual groom, Casimir Dudevant, twenty-seven, was no great shakes in the suitor department, yet at eighteen she happily succumbed. A son, Maurice, was soon born, named after her beloved father, and later a daughter, Solange.

It seemed that hers would be no more than the life of a rural landowner’s wife. But “Aurore, of course, does not yet know that she will become George Sand,” writes Sampson, “and consort with some of the most brilliant minds of her day.”

Fast forward to Paris, 1838. Just as Aurore Dupin has thoroughly metamorphised into George Sand, Chopin, a Polish refugee, has changed his given name from Fryderyk to Frédéric. Long divorced from Dudevant, Sand finished with her sexual adventures and is ready again for a more solid attachment. But the man with whom she would spend nine years of her life hadn’t been impressed on first meeting her. “What an unappealing woman, this Sand,” he was reported as saying. “Is it truly a woman? I’m ready to doubt this.”

Most of Sand’s many lovers were male (and as a rule several years younger), though she was known to have had at least one female partner. Chopin’s deeply romantic attachments were predominantly with men. Yet by early 1838 he and Sand were cohabiting, with Chopin perpetually ill with bronchitis, possibly tubercular, and Sand given over to nursing and financially supporting him.

Seeking accommodation in sunnier places than wintry, smoke-filled Paris, they travelled throughout the Mediterranean, the effort compounded by the arduous business of finding him a decent piano. After all that, Mallorca, where they finally settled, proved far too windy for Chopin’s feeble lungs, though Sand, ever driven for the funds to sustain them both (and various other members of their entourage) could write just about anywhere — on top of her many domestic responsibilities. As Sampson writes, “Like his future admirers, the musician seems to take it for granted that even a woman of George’s international standing and unconventionality will put the man’s work first.”

At this stage we need to be reminded of Sand’s fearsome intelligence, the prodigiousness of her output — no fewer than seventy novels, numerous collections of works and an esteemed autobiography, not to mention her plays — or the standing she attained in her lifetime as one of France’s most eminent writers. She had her detractors, but it’s important to remember how, on her arrival in Paris as a young woman in her late twenties, she took the literary establishment by storm.

The male attire, the cigars, the name (taken from her lover Jules Sandeau, with whom she collaborated on her first novel) — these were not merely performative, as we would call them today, but were necessary passports to the exclusively male publishing houses of the 1830s. Importantly too — and like many high achievers then and now — she also landed in the right place at just the right time.

Soon some of Paris’s most important critics were taking her under their wing. In a text-dominated age she quickly became as famous as an actor or musician might a century later. On her death in 1876 no less a figure than Gustave Flaubert pronounced: “One had to know her as I did to know how much of the feminine was in that great man [sic], the immensity of tenderness in that genius. Her name will live in unique glory as one of the great figures of France.”

Still, as a contemporary of Victor Hugo and Honoré de Balzac, or of Flaubert himself, her place in the literary canon has not been secure. And even while she was alive she had detractors whose remarks could be deeply misogynistic and graphic, many alluding to her bodily fluids, ‘ink-pisser’ being the mildest of them. (Julia Gillard could be gratified to learn that she’s not the only woman to be publicly lampooned for the size of her bottom.)

I confess I’m hard put to cover the breadth and depth of so full a life as Sampson presents us. Perhaps we have to return to Aurore’s childhood to find an explanation for her subjecting herself so consistently to the needs of her lovers, particularly Chopin. Perhaps the loss of her beloved father when she was only four was the source of her predilection for younger men and her eschewing more alpha males.

But she was born too early for psychoanalysis to explain it and Sampson isn’t tempted to go there. Instead she makes a compelling case for Sand’s being ahead of her time, both in her feminism and in her sensitivity to ecological issues, the latter reflecting the years she spent at her beloved Nohant, the place where Chopin found the serenity to compose some of the finest pieces of his oeuvre (and is now maintained as a museum in her honour).

Sampson herself is a many-honoured British poet and biographer who began her working life as a musician, which led her first to Chopin and through him to Sand. Her prodigious and varied output— her previous biographies include In Search of Mary Shelley: The Girl Who Wrote Frankenstein and Two-Way Mirror: The Life of Elizabeth Barrett Browning — has established her as a doyenne of English letters.

I hadn’t known of either of those other works when Becoming George was offered to me to review, but on the basis of what she’s written here I’ll certainly seek them out. Not only because of my interest in their subjects, but because of the intriguing colloquialism of Sampson’s style, unlike that of any other literary biographer’s I’ve come across: her skilful use of contractions, and how fluidly she moves from past to present tense throughout the narrative. Also striking are the eight intervening chapters in which Sampson discusses black-and-white portraits of Sand, each of which lends further dimension to her subject’s development at different stages of her life.

It should be clear by now how much Becoming George impressed me. English translations of some of Sand’s work are available, mostly online, and other accounts of her life include the recent graphic biography by Séverine Vidal, now also in English. How wonderful to think that centuries later Aurore Dupin is finally getting the attention she deserves. It’s a long time to wait, but I for one will be attempting a brush-up of my high school French on the strength of it. •
